content: Surfaces of buildings can be constructed using various materials such as brick, stucco, wood, stone, cement or concrete blocks, asbestos, vinyl, or other materials. A deficiency in protective treatment is identified when there is a split, separation, or gap in the exterior walls. If there is uncertainty about the severity of the condition, it is recommended to request an inspection by a structural engineer. Chimneys and towers are considered deficient if the chimney, including the portion extending above the roofline, has separated from the wall or exhibits cracks, spalling, missing pieces, or broken sections. Exterior wall surfaces are deemed deficient if there is evidence of deterioration, such as missing pieces, holes, or spalling. The Healthy Housing Inspection Manual was developed to provide a comprehensive approach to addressing housing deficiencies that impact health and safety. It aims to broaden the scope of public health and safety programs, such as those targeting childhood lead poisoning prevention, residential asthma intervention, and injury prevention, by addressing multiple housing deficiencies holistically. The manual also seeks to build competency among professionals such as environmental public health practitioners, public health nurses, housing specialists, property owners, and managers, enabling them to incorporate healthy housing activities into their work. National capacity for healthy housing is being developed through grants, contracts, and other activities at federal, state, tribal, and community levels. These initiatives focus on researching and demonstrating cost-effective methods for assessing and mitigating home hazards. Educational and outreach materials are being developed to raise public awareness of residential hazards, particularly for high-risk populations, and to provide actionable steps households can take to reduce risks of illness and injury. The Healthy Housing Inspection Manual serves as a reference tool for local jurisdictions and other stakeholders. It is designed to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of public health, housing management, and workforce efforts in identifying, preventing, and controlling health problems associated with housing. The manual does not introduce new inspection requirements or modify existing ones for housing agencies, residents, HUD, or CDC. It is not a substitute for the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) Minimum Property Standards and does not establish regulatory authority for HUD or CDC regarding residential inspection requirements. The manual guides environmental health professionals, housing managers, specialists, and inspectors through the elements of a holistic home inspection. It is also a valuable resource for nurses, outreach workers, and others interested in preventing illness and injury caused by residential health and safety hazards. The manual addresses a wide range of housing deficiencies and hazards that can affect residents' health and safety. Its purpose is to improve communication and collaboration among public health professionals, housing professionals, property owners, and managers. It also aims to enhance understanding of the relationships between exposure to hazardous agents, home conditions, and adverse health outcomes, while improving program efficiency in addressing housing deficiencies. HUD and CDC have jointly developed and funded other activities related to healthy homes, including a curriculum for training environmental public health practitioners, public health nurses, housing specialists, and others in addressing housing-related health hazards. The manual recommends starting with the Healthy Housing Model Resident Questionnaire, a voluntary health assessment tool, to collect information that cannot be determined visually. This questionnaire can provide important clues about housing deficiencies. The Visual Assessment Data Collection Form should then be used to gather information that can be determined without questioning residents. This form includes detailed assessments of exterior housing, kitchens, bathrooms, living areas, and general building information. The manual includes three supporting appendices: A data dictionary defining housing deficiencies listed in the Visual Assessment Data Collection Form. A cross-reference to code provisions in the 2003 International Property Maintenance Code (IPMC). Additional resources, such as links to environmental sampling methods and information on substances or issues related to healthy housing. The Healthy Homes Model Resident Questionnaire can be adapted by local jurisdictions to meet specific needs. It is important to follow local regulations for collecting and safeguarding personal data. The questionnaire may include questions about ownership or rental status, contact information for the building owner, whether the building is privately owned or managed by a public housing authority, and whether government subsidies are involved. Injuries occurring in the past three months should be documented, including details about the circumstances, objects, substances, or people involved, and what the injured person was doing at the time. Poisonings in the home, such as those caused by swallowing or inhaling harmful substances like bleach, carbon monoxide, or excessive medications, should be recorded. Food poisoning, sun poisoning, and poison ivy are excluded. For each building or housing development, observations should be completed for the site, exterior and building systems, common areas, and individual units. Specific locations of hazards can be recorded in the comments section. Playground equipment should have at least 12 inches of safety-tested materials like wood chips, mulch, sand, pea gravel, or rubber mats. Equipment that is dangerous or broken should be reported immediately to building management or owners. Fire exits must be accessible and functional. Any part of a fire escape that is blocked, improperly marked, or unusable due to conditions like nailed-shut windows or chained panic hardware is considered deficient. Electrical systems must safely provide power throughout the building. Deficiencies include blocked access, burnt or missing breakers, evidence of leaks or corrosion, frayed wiring, and missing covers. Environmental sampling for contaminants should be conducted carefully and in compliance with local regulations. Proper training and consultation with professionals are recommended before undertaking sampling. The manual emphasizes the importance of following manufacturer instructions for sampling instruments and does not endorse specific products or methods. Additional sampling procedures may be recommended based on individual situations.
